stem: The first step of a typical scientific investigation is to
a: publish a conclusion with no question
b: ask a clear question or identify a problem
d: change the data to fit a belief
explanation: Research starts from a question that can be investigated. The conclusion comes after evidence has been collected and examined.
A hypothesis states what the researcher thinks may be true, in a form that evidence can support or contradict. It is not yet a settled law.

stem: An independent variable is the factor that the researcher
explanation: The independent variable is the input that is changed. The dependent variable is the outcome that is measured.

c: the factor the researcher deliberately changes
explanation: The dependent variable responds to the change under study. For example, rainfall might be measured while the season, the independent factor, changes.

stem: A control in an experiment is used to
a: provide a comparison in which the factor under test is absent or unchanged
explanation: The control shows what happens without the treatment. The difference between control and treatment is the evidence.

a: the entire population in every case
explanation: Researchers usually cannot measure every member of a population, so they study a sample and generalise with care.

c: the whole group about which a conclusion is wanted
d: only the people in one city
explanation: The population is the full set of interest, such as all days in a climate record. A sample is the part actually observed.

a: no list is needed and choice is secret
b: every member has a known chance of being chosen
c: the researcher picks only favourable cases
d: the first item is always chosen
explanation: In a simple random sample, each member has an equal chance. Choosing only convenient or favourable cases is bias, not random sampling.

stem: Bias in a sample means the sample
c: has no error of any kind
d: is the same as a census
explanation: A biased sample leans in one direction, so averages drawn from it can be misleading. A large sample can still be biased if the method of selection is poor.
The mean is the sum divided by the number of values. The middle value is the median, and the most frequent value is the mode.

c: the middle value when the data are ordered
explanation: Order the observations and take the middle one. The median is less pulled by a single extreme value than the mean is.
If 12 mm appears more often than any other rainfall amount in a list, 12 mm is the mode.

stem: The range of a data set is
a: the largest value minus the smallest
explanation: Range is a simple measure of spread. A set running from 2 to 20 has a range of 18.

stem: A null hypothesis usually states that
a: the researcher's favourite result is already true
b: the data need not be collected
d: there is no effect, or no difference
explanation: The null is the default claim of no difference. Evidence is then used to see whether that claim should be rejected.

a: the sample is the whole population
d: one variable has been proved to cause the other
explanation: A correlation shows an association. It does not by itself prove that one variable causes the other.

b: a change in one variable brings about a change in another
c: two lines on a graph look similar for any reason
d: a sample was chosen at random
explanation: Cause is a stronger claim than association. An experiment or a careful design is usually needed before a cause is accepted.

a: collected by the researcher for the study
b: only data published by someone else
explanation: A rainfall record the researcher measures is primary data. A table copied from an earlier report is secondary data.
Census tables, published climate normals, and earlier papers are secondary sources. They were gathered for another purpose or by another person.
Rainfall in millimetres and temperature in degrees are quantitative. Descriptions in words, without numbers, are qualitative.
A description of cloud type in words is qualitative. A measured cloud-base height in metres is quantitative.

b: it measures a different concept each time
explanation: A reliable instrument or procedure is consistent. Validity is the separate question of whether it measures the right thing.

a: the same wrong result every time
b: the sample is as small as possible
d: the method measures what it is intended to measure
explanation: A test can be reliable but still invalid if it consistently measures the wrong quantity. Validity is about being on target.

c: a value far from the other observations
explanation: An outlier lies well outside the cluster of the rest of the data. It may be a real extreme or an error, so it should be checked rather than ignored automatically.

stem: A census differs from a sample because a census
b: attempts to include every member of the population
explanation: A census is a complete enumeration. A sample studies only part of the population.

stem: Peer review means that a report is
a: examined by other experts before publication
explanation: Independent specialists check the methods and claims. Review reduces, but does not remove, the chance of error.

d: a survey of existing research on the topic
explanation: Before new work, the researcher reads what is already known. That summary of earlier studies is the literature review.

c: presenting someone else's work as one's own
explanation: Using another person's words or ideas without acknowledgement is plagiarism. Proper citation avoids it.

b: a reference to the source of information
explanation: A citation tells the reader where a fact or quotation came from, so the claim can be checked.

stem: In a graph of rainfall against month, the dependent variable is usually
explanation: Rainfall is the outcome being shown, so it is plotted as the dependent variable, often on the vertical axis. Month is the independent variable.

stem: A bar chart is suitable for
a: showing the chemical formula of ozone only
explanation: Bars compare quantities across categories, such as rainfall by month. The scale must be shown so the lengths can be read.

stem: A line graph is often used to show
explanation: A line connects values in order, so it shows a trend, such as temperature through the year.

b: estimating a value between known points
c: inventing a value far outside the data with no caution
explanation: If rainfall is known for June and August, estimating July from those neighbours is interpolation. Estimating beyond the last point is extrapolation.

a: extending a pattern beyond the range of the data
b: reading a value that was measured directly
explanation: Extrapolation continues a trend outside the observations. It is less secure than interpolation because the pattern may change.

stem: A significant figure in a measurement reflects
d: the precision with which the number is known
explanation: Writing 12.0 mm claims more precision than writing 12 mm. Digits that are justified by the measurement are significant figures.

stem: Rounding 16.48 to the nearest whole number gives
explanation: The first decimal digit is 4, which is less than 5, so the whole number stays 16. A digit of 5 or more would round the number up.

stem: A percentage error compares the error with
explanation: Percentage error is the absolute error divided by the accepted value, multiplied by 100. It shows the size of the mistake relative to the quantity itself.

a: an independent worker can obtain a similar result
d: only one person may ever try it
explanation: A scientific result should be obtainable again by someone who follows the method. That is why methods must be reported.

stem: An abstract of a paper is
d: a short summary of the work
explanation: The abstract states the question, method, and main findings in a few paragraphs so a reader can see the point quickly.

stem: A variable that is held constant is called
explanation: Controlled variables are kept the same so they do not confuse the result. Only the independent variable is deliberately changed.

stem: A double-blind trial is one in which
a: the hypothesis is hidden from the author forever
b: neither the participant nor the observer knows who received the treatment
c: everyone knows the result in advance
explanation: Keeping both sides unaware reduces bias in how the treatment is given and how the outcome is judged. It is common in medical trials.

stem: Informed consent means that a participant
a: agrees after being told what the study involves
c: must be paid double the mean
explanation: People should know the nature of a study and freely agree to take part. Including them in secret is not informed consent.

b: a single average with no dates
d: a sequence of observations in time order
explanation: Monthly rainfall from 1990 to 2020 is a time series. Order in time is essential.

stem: A moving average is used to
c: smooth short-term ups and downs in a series
explanation: Averaging neighbouring values reduces noise so a longer trend is easier to see. It does not remove the need to look at the original data.

b: how spread out the values are around the mean
explanation: A small standard deviation means the values cluster near the mean. A large one means they are widely scattered.

stem: If two data sets have the same mean but one has a larger standard deviation, that set is
explanation: The means match, so the typical level is similar. The larger standard deviation shows greater scatter about that mean.

stem: A scatter plot is used to look for
d: a relationship between two numerical variables
explanation: Each point has two coordinates, such as temperature and humidity. The pattern of points suggests whether the variables move together.

stem: A conclusion in a report should
a: introduce new measurements that were never made
explanation: The conclusion answers the research question using the results. Claims that the data do not support do not belong there.

stem: An anomaly in a climate series is
b: the difference between a value and the long-term average
explanation: A temperature anomaly of +1°C means that month was one degree warmer than the chosen normal. Anomalies make departures from the usual climate easy to see.

a: repeating the trial so the result is not based on one case
b: doing the trial once and stopping
explanation: Several repeats show whether a result is stable or a one-off accident. A single trial is a weak basis for a general claim.

stem: The best description of the scientific attitude to a favoured hypothesis is that it should be
d: tested and given up if the evidence is against it
explanation: A hypothesis is useful only if it can fail. When careful evidence contradicts it, the hypothesis is revised or rejected.
